metadata.title: Good Citizenship and Youth: Understanding … (ICCS 2016-based chapters on citizenship norms and related outcomes)
metadata.venue: IEA Research for Education 12 (Springer/IEA book chapters)

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The analyses use ICCS 2016’s complex two-stage stratified sampling design with schools as the primary sampling unit and intact classrooms sampled within schools. The book chapters explicitly state that all estimates incorporate the ICCS 2016 survey design, including Taylor Series Linearization for sampling variance estimation and corrections for clustering to avoid Type I error inflation. For cross-country comparability, survey weights were rescaled so that countries contribute equally to point estimates; in multilevel models, weights were further scaled to the effective sample size. In the latent class/profile chapters, scaled survey weights (up to 1000) are used and standard errors are obtained via Taylor Series Linearization with schools as the primary sampling unit and jackzones as pseudo strata.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: The chapters use ICCS 2016 IRT-based scale scores and, in some chapters, civic knowledge is represented using plausible values (e.g., PV1CIV) or WLE/theta-like IRT scores. However, the provided text does not describe a specific missing-data procedure for the PVs (e.g., whether missing items were imputed, deleted, or handled via multiple imputation). Given that the book reports that selected variables have low missingness (e.g., <5% in one chapter) but does not specify the exact missing-data handling method, the missing-data strategy cannot be classified reliably from the excerpt.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: The empirical chapters use ICCS 2016 grade 8 student responses from 24 participating countries/regions (Europe, Latin America, and Asia) and, for specific chapters, restrict to subsets: (i) Latin America chapters use the five Latin American countries (Chile, Colombia, Dominican Republic, Mexico, Peru); (ii) European chapters restrict to nine European countries/regions participating in the European module and further require immigrant subsample sizes above N=200; (iii) the school-effectiveness chapter uses the full 24-country sample with grade 8 students and includes variables with <5% missingness. For the latent class/profile construction, the model is fitted on 12 citizenship-norm items with binary recoding (important vs not important) and uses a structurally homogeneous multigroup latent class model; classification quality is assessed via modal classification probabilities. For multilevel models, student and school means are used for school-level predictors, and country fixed effects/dummy-coded country intercepts are included; weights are rescaled to ensure equal country contribution.

The core measurement approach uses a multigroup latent class model to generate five citizenship norms profiles (comprehensive, socially engaged, duty-based, monitorial, anomic) from 12 ICCS citizenship-norm items, with binary recoding of importance. Across chapters, outcomes include profile membership (modeled with multilevel multinomial logistic regression), support for authoritarian government practices (modeled with clustered regression using IRT/WLE scores), tolerance of corruption (modeled with multilevel models using IRT-based tolerance scores), and political tolerance (modeled with multiple-group multinomial logistic regression). The analyses explicitly incorporate ICCS’s complex sampling design using Taylor Series Linearization and rescaled survey weights to ensure equal country contribution; however, the excerpt does not provide a complete missing-data procedure for PVs/IRT scores, so missing-data handling cannot be fully audited. Overall, the findings emphasize that civic learning opportunities and open classroom discussion are consistently associated with more comprehensive citizenship norms and lower tolerance of corruption/authoritarianism, though the comparative approach is correlational and does not establish causality.
